html:
The Akimel O'odham, "River People", are the O'odham of the middle Gila and Salt rivers in central Arizona, known to the Spanish as the Pima. They see themselves as heirs of the Hohokam, who dug large irrigation canals in the same valleys until about 1450.

They farmed with canals of their own, growing maize, beans, squash, cotton and later wheat. The Jesuit Eusebio Kino visited them in the 1690s. In the 1850s their villages sold food to travellers heading for California, and the Gila River reservation was set up in 1859. Soon after, upstream settlers took the Gila's water; the fields dried up and the late 1800s became known as the years of famine. With the Maricopa they share the Gila River and Salt River communities. Their kin the Tohono O'odham, the "Desert People", live to the south.
